content: Headgear is an orthodontic appliance that is attached to dental braces to address severe bite problems. It is most commonly used to correct anteroposterior discrepancies, such as when the upper teeth are positioned too far forward relative to the lower teeth, a condition known as increased overjet. The headgear is connected to the braces using metal hooks or a facebow and is anchored at the back of the head or neck with straps or a head-cap. Elastic bands are typically employed to exert pressure on the bow or hooks. The primary function of headgear is to slow down or halt the growth of the upper jaw, thereby preventing or correcting an overjet. Another type of headgear is designed to treat reverse overjets, where the upper jaw is not sufficiently forward. This appliance, resembling a facemask, is also attached to braces and promotes forward growth of the upper jaw. Headgear can also be used to create additional space for teeth to erupt. It is attached to the molars using molar headgear bands and tubes, helping to retract the molars and create space for the front teeth to be moved backward with braces and bands. Initially, wearing headgear can be embarrassing for children, but most orthodontists agree that children and adolescents adapt quickly to these changes and requirements. The appliance typically needs to be worn for 16 to 22 hours a day, although some orthodontists may only require 12 hours of wear, often during the night. Patients may also need additional appliances and accessories, such as coil springs, plates, retainers, and elastic bands, to complement the headgear. While the majority of patients undergoing this treatment are children and adolescents, adults may also be required to wear such appliances in certain cases. Headgear remains a valuable tool for orthodontic specialists, especially as fewer orthodontists use temporary anchorage devices (TADs) inside the mouth to achieve similar tooth movements. A facemask, also known as reverse-pull headgear, is an orthodontic appliance typically used in growing patients to correct underbites, classified as Class III orthodontic problems. It works by pulling the upper jaw (maxilla) forward and assisting its growth, allowing it to catch up with the lower jaw (mandible). For the appliance to be effective, it must be worn for approximately 12 to 22 hours daily over a period of 6 to 18 months, depending on the severity of the bite and the patient’s growth rate. The facemask consists of a frame or center bars that are strapped to the patient’s head during a fitting appointment. The frame includes a section positioned in front of the patient’s mouth, which allows for the attachment of elastic or rubber bands that connect directly to the braces or other oral appliances in the mouth. These elastics create a forward-pulling force to move the upper jaw forward. The orthodontic facemask is composed of three main components: 1. Face Frame: The face frame is a metal and plastic structure adjusted to fit the patient’s face. It is stabilized on the child’s face using a padded chin cup and forehead pad for comfort. The frame includes a mouth-yoke, which the orthodontist adjusts to position it in front of the patient’s mouth. The mouth-yoke has several hooks (typically 4 to 6) that allow the orthodontist to attach elastics or springs directly into the patient’s mouth. The frame permits free head movement and talking, but other oral activities are restricted. Drinking is recommended through a straw to avoid removing the appliance during the day or night. 2. Head-Cap: Some facemasks and all reverse-pull headgear include a head-cap, which consists of straps that fit around the patient’s head. The head-cap stabilizes the face frame and ensures it is held correctly in position. 3. Attachment: The final component is the mouth attachment, which typically uses rubber bands, elastics, or springs to connect the facemask from the mouth-yoke into the patient’s mouth. The elastics hook onto the child’s braces or other suitable oral appliances. Up to six elastics may be used to provide various forward and sideways forces on the teeth and dental arch while still allowing the patient to open and close their jaws. In some cases, surgery may be required in conjunction with a facemask or reverse-pull headgear. However, many parents and doctors advocate for early intervention (ages 7 to 13) with a facemask to avoid costly and invasive surgical procedures later. The appliance is highly effective in correcting Class III orthodontic problems in younger or adolescent patients who are still growing. Parents should consult their orthodontist for detailed information tailored to their child’s needs. Initially, children may find it challenging to wear a facemask or headgear, but most doctors and parents agree that children and adolescents adapt quickly to these changes and requirements.
